title: Ship your first change with GitHub Flow
summary: Create a repository, make a branch and a commit in the browser, then merge it through a pull request — the full GitHub Flow loop.

steps.instructions: Create a new public repository named `first-flow` with a README — see [creating a repository](creating-a-repository).
In the browser, open `README.md`, click the pencil, add one sentence, and choose **Create a new branch** when committing; name the branch `feature/intro`.
On the "Open a pull request" prompt, write a title and a body using Markdown: one `## What changed` heading and one task-list item.
Open the pull request, review the **Files changed** tab, then merge it with a merge commit.
Delete the branch when GitHub offers to; confirm `main` now carries your sentence.
Clone the repository locally (`git clone` your repo URL), create branch `feature/local-edit`, edit any file, and run `git add` → `git commit` → `git push -u origin feature/local-edit`.
Open a second pull request from your machine’s branch and merge it.

outcomes: Repository `first-flow` exists with a merged pull request on `main`.
Two closed PRs appear under the Pull requests tab, one from the web editor and one from a local clone.
The branch list shows no leftover `feature/*` branches after merges.
checks: Open the repository’s **Insights → Pulse** and find both merges recorded in the last week ([about repository graphs](about-repository-graphs)).
Run `git log --oneline` locally and find the two merge commits on `main`.
Visit your pull request and confirm the issue-style Markdown (heading, task list) rendered in the body.

title: Give a repository a proper community profile
summary: Add the key community files — README, LICENSE, CONTRIBUTING, CODEOWNERS, and an issue template — then read the Community Standards checklist.

steps.instructions: In repo `first-flow` (or any repo you own), add a `LICENSE` file via **Add file → Create new file**, choosing a license from the chooser; see [licensing a repository](licensing-a-repository).
Create `CONTRIBUTING.md` with three short sections: how to propose a change, code style, and what a good issue contains ([setting guidelines](contributing-guidelines)).
Create `.github/CODEOWNERS` mapping `/README.md @your-username` and `/` to yourself ([about code owners](about-code-owners)).
Create `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.md` with a template body — repro steps, expected, actual ([about templates](issue-pr-templates)).
Create `SECURITY.md` with a contact for vulnerability reports ([add a security policy](add-security-policy)).
Open **Insights → Community** and read the Community Standards checklist.
Star the repository and open **Insights** to see where stars and traffic appear ([about repository graphs](about-repository-graphs)).

outcomes: The Community Standards checklist shows all key files present and green.
Editing `README.md` in a new PR auto-requests you as reviewer via CODEOWNERS.
Creating a new issue offers your bug report template.
checks: Open **Insights → Community** and confirm every section is checked, with links to each file.
Start a new PR changing `README.md` and confirm the reviewers list pre-fills from CODEOWNERS.
Click **New issue** and confirm the bug-report template appears as an option, then cancel.

title: Link an issue to a pull request and close it by merging
summary: File an issue, fix it on a branch, and let a closing keyword in the pull request do the bookkeeping — then tune notifications.

steps.instructions: Open a new issue titled "Fix typo in README" with a label and yourself as assignee ([about issues](about-issues)).
Create branch `fix/readme-typo`, correct the typo, and commit to the branch.
Open a pull request whose description contains `Closes #1` (use your issue’s real number) — see [linking a pull request to an issue](linking-pr-to-issue).
Confirm the PR sidebar shows the issue linked under "Development".
Merge the pull request into `main` and watch the issue close automatically.
In the repo’s **Watch** dropdown (top right), set a custom watch level; then check your [notification settings](about-notifications) under personal settings → notifications.
Filter your issues list with `is:closed is:issue reason:completed` to see the auto-closed issue ([filtering and searching](filtering-issues)).

outcomes: The issue is closed by the merge, with a back-reference to the PR.
The PR shows the issue in its Development section before merge.
Your watch level for the repo is set deliberately, not by default.
checks: Open the closed issue and confirm the timeline says it was closed by the PR merge, not manually.
Open the merged PR and confirm the linked-issue badge in the sidebar.
Visit the notifications inbox (web) and find one notification generated by this exercise.

title: Run your first workflow and meet the modern surfaces
summary: Enable a starter GitHub Actions workflow on a branch, read its run log, then open the same repo in a codespace and in github.dev.

steps.instructions: In your repo, open the **Actions** tab and enable a starter workflow on a new branch (any suggested "simple" workflow) — see [GitHub Actions docs](gh-docs-actions).
Merge the branch’s PR (or run the workflow on the branch) and open the run from the Actions list.
Read the run: find the job, expand one step, and locate the log line that prints your runner’s operating system.
Press `.` on any repository page (or swap `github.com` → `github.dev`) to open the web editor — [github.dev](githubdev-editor).
Edit any file in github.dev, open the Source Control panel, and commit to a branch.
From the **Code** button, open the repo in a Codespace — [what are Codespaces](what-are-codespaces).
In the codespace terminal run `git status`, then stop the codespace from the codespaces list.

outcomes: One completed workflow run visible under the Actions tab with green checks.
A commit made from github.dev on a branch.
A stopped codespace listed under your account (not deleted, not running).
checks: In the workflow run, confirm each step’s log expands and the runner name appears ([GitHub Actions docs](gh-docs-actions)).
In github.dev, confirm the editor opened your repository files without a running environment.
On [your codespaces list](codespaces-list) confirm the codespace state is "Stopped" to avoid idle billing.

title: Plan work with a Project, labels, and milestones
summary: Build an organization Project with table and board views, wire labels and a milestone to issues, and let built-in automation do the sorting.

steps.instructions: Create a new Project (organization-level or user-level) and add two of your existing issues plus one draft item — [about Projects](about-projects).
Add a single-select field `Status` with columns Backlog / In progress / Done.
Create a second view with the **board** layout grouped by Status — see [changing the layout of a view](project-view-layouts).
Add a milestone "v0.1" with a due date and assign it to both issues ([about milestones](about-milestones)).
Create or edit a label `docs` and apply it to one issue ([managing labels](managing-labels)).
Enable a built-in automation, such as "auto-move to Done when the item closes" — [using the built-in automations](built-in-automations).
Close one linked issue and reopen the Project to see the automation move it.

outcomes: A Project with at least a table view and a board view over the same items.
A milestone showing partial completion (one closed, one open issue).
The closed issue moved to Done without you dragging it.
checks: Switch between the two views and confirm the same items appear with different layouts.
Open the milestone and confirm its progress bar counts exactly your two issues.
Open **Insights** on the project and confirm a chart renders from your items ([about insights](about-project-insights)).

title: Harden a repository: 2FA, permissions, branch protection
summary: Verify your account’s 2FA/passkey state, exercise collaborator permissions, and enforce branch protection on `main`.

steps.instructions: Open personal **Settings → Password and authentication** and confirm 2FA is active; note whether a passkey is registered — [configuring 2FA](configure-2fa), [about passkeys](about-passkeys).

In your repo’s **Settings → Collaborators**, note that personal collaborators get write access (the single rung on personal repos) — contrast with [repository roles](repository-roles) in organizations.
Under **Settings → Branches**, add a branch protection rule for `main` ([about protected branches](about-protected-branches)): require a pull request before merging, with one approval.
Require status checks (pick any check if one exists from lab 04) and enable "Do not allow bypassing the above settings".
Try to push a commit directly to `main` from your local clone.
Check the repo’s visibility setting under **Settings → General** — read [setting repository visibility](setting-repository-visibility) for what changes when visibility flips.
If you have an organization: create a team, add yourself, and grant the team `read` on a repo — [about teams](about-teams).

outcomes: Branch protection on `main` with required review and checks.
A rejected direct push to `main` with a protection-message from GitHub.
Team-based access visible in the repo’s Collaborators and teams settings (org step only).
checks: Run `git push origin main` locally and confirm GitHub rejects it, quoting the branch protection rule.
Open **Settings → Branches** and confirm the rule lists `main` with both protections ticked.
Open your authentication settings page and point to where 2FA methods and passkeys are listed.

title: Contribute upstream: fork, propose, polish
summary: Fork a real open source repository, propose a documentation change upstream, and tour Sponsors and the Marketplace.

steps.instructions: Pick a small active open source repo you use (or your own second repo) and fork it — [about forks](about-forks).
In your fork, create branch `docs/clarify-readme` and improve one sentence of the README.
Open a pull request **against the upstream repository** (not your fork’s `main`).
On the upstream repo, check its contribution path: CONTRIBUTING file, good first issue labels — see [finding ways to contribute](ways-to-contribute).
Visit the profile of the upstream maintainer and open their **Sponsors** section — [GitHub Sponsors](github-sponsors).
Open [GitHub Marketplace](github-marketplace) and browse one CI app and one Action; note install permissions before closing the page.
Follow the maintainer ([following people](following-people)) and confirm the feed shows their public activity on your dashboard.

outcomes: A fork under your account with one branch ahead of upstream.
An open (or merged) upstream PR from your fork.
A follow on the maintainer reflected in your home feed.
checks: Open the upstream PR and confirm the base repository is upstream, not your fork.
Confirm your fork page shows "forked from <upstream>" at the top.
Open your GitHub dashboard and find one public activity card from the maintainer you followed.
